20          Plaintiff Inventec Corporation (“Plaintiff” or “Inventec”) brings this Complaint against
21   Defendant X Corp. (“Defendant” or “X Corp.”) and alleges as follows:
22                                             NATURE OF ACTION
23          1.      According to numerous press reports and filed lawsuits, and on information and belief,
24   following Elon Musk’s takeover of the company in October 2022, X Corp., formerly Twitter, Inc.
25   (“Twitter” or “X Corp.”) has refused to honor numerous agreements with its vendors and suppliers.
26   This lawsuit involves one of those suppliers, Inventec, a global manufacturer of computers, servers,
27   notebooks, and other products in the wireless communication field, and X Corp.’s failure and refusal
28   to pay Inventec for components that Inventec procured for X Corp., which X Corp. agreed to take

      COMPLAINT                                          1
                                                                                                  110114977
             Case 3:26-cv-05145         Document 1        Filed 05/29/26      Page 2 of 16




 1   responsibility for. As a result of X Corp.’s contractual breaches and failure to pay for goods and

 2   components, Inventec has been damaged in an amount of at least $30,000,000.00.

 3                                                  PARTIES

 4          2.      Inventec is, and at all relevant times was, a corporation duly organized and existing

 5   under the laws of the country of the Republic of China also known as Taiwan, with its principal place

 6   of business in Taipei, Taiwan.

 7          3.      Upon information and belief, Defendant X Corp. is a corporation organized and

 8   existing under the laws of Nevada, with its principal place of business in Bastrop, Texas.

 9          4.      At all relevant times, X Corp. transacted business within the Northern District of

10   California.

11                                      JURISDICTION AND VENUE

12          5.      This Court possesses diversity jurisdiction under 28 U.S.C. § 1332, as Inventec is a

13   citizen of Taiwan and X Corp. is a citizen of Nevada and Texas. There is complete diversity of

14   citizenship between Inventec and X Corp., and the amount in controversy exceeds $75,000.

15          6.      This Court has personal jurisdiction over X Corp. pursuant to a binding jurisdiction

16   clause within an agreement giving rise to the present dispute that was negotiated and executed by the

17   parties, which states that “[a]ny legal action or proceeding arising under this Agreement will be

18   brought exclusively in the federal or state courts located in the Northern District of California, in the

19   city of San Francisco, and the parties hereby irrevocably consent to the personal jurisdiction and venue

20   therein.” Further, this Court has personal jurisdiction over X Corp. because at all relevant times, it

21   has conducted commercial activities within the State of California that are substantial, continuous, and

22   systematic.

23          7.      Venue is proper under 28 U.S.C. § 1391(b) and based on X Corp.’s express prior

24   consent in the agreement to the venue of this Court. Further, venue is proper in this District because

25   a substantial part of the events, acts and omissions giving rise to the claims occurred in this District.

26

27

28

                                                                                                       110114977

 1                                       FACTUAL ALLEGATIONS

 2           8.     Founded in 1975, Inventec is a leading global manufacturer of computers, telephones,

 3   notebooks, servers, and products related to cloud computing, wireless communication, and intelligent

 4   devices.

 5           9.     Inventec is also a leading original equipment manufacturer (“OEM”) and original

 6   design manufacturer (“ODM”) company for such products. Inventec also makes and sells products

 7   under its own label.

 8           10.    Inventec sells highly customized products designed pursuant to their clients’ unique

 9   specifications. Inventec also designs products based on their clients’ unique specifications, and

10   produces and sells those products to clients on a private label or white label basis so that clients may

11   conserve resources by not having to invest in manufacturing products themselves.

12           11.    Inventec manufactures and designs, among numerous other products, server racks,

13   which are open frames or cabinets designed for organizing and securing information technology (“IT”)

14   equipment.

15           12.    Those racks often include specific network switches, which are networking hardware

16   that connect devices on a computer network by forwarding data between devices; a network switch

17   allows multiple IT devices to communicate with one another.

18           13.    X Corp. is a social media company that operates the internet site of the same name, and

19   which engaged Inventec to design X Corp.’s specifications and manufacture non-standard server racks

20   for its use.

21           14.    On or about December 13, 2020, Inventec and X Corp. entered into a Master Purchase

22   Agreement (“MPA”) pursuant to which Inventec agreed to sell and deliver various products to X

23   Corp., including, as relevant here, non-standard server racks and switches. A true and correct copy of

24   the Master Purchase Agreement is attached hereto as Exhibit A.

25           15.    The racks were custom manufactured by Inventec to X Corp.’s unique specifications

26   and therefore constitute non-standard components.

27           16.    Given the long lead time to procure components for non-standard racks, including

28   switches, it is standard industry practice and necessary for ODM’s like Inventec to procure

      COMPLAINT                                         3
                                                                                                     110114977
             Case 3:26-cv-05145        Document 1        Filed 05/29/26     Page 4 of 16




 1   components well in advance of the anticipated delivery date of the racks. This includes non-standard

 2   components such as those that are at issue in this case.

 3          17.     Accordingly, Section 4.4 of the Master Purchase Agreement holds X Corp. liable for

 4   cancellations of certain components. Specifically, it provides:

 5          4.4     Forecast. Forecast provided by Twitter for Supplier’s standard Components
            are non-binding. For non-standard Components (any components that are customized
 6          per Twitter’s request), Twitter anticipates providing Supplier with a three-month
            rolling forecast.
 7

 8          18.     Notably, Section 4.4 expressly states that forecasts are not binding on X Corp. as to

 9   standard components. However, this provision did not state that forecasts were not binding on X Corp.

10   as to non-standard components; instead, the risk of loss as to non-standard components would fall on

11   X Corp. by negative inference—if X Corp. was not intended to bear the risk of loss as to non-standard

12   components, Section 4.4 would have expressly stated as much just as it did for standard components.

13          19.     The course of performance and course of dealing between the parties over the years

14   further confirms their mutual understanding that X Corp.’s forecasts for non-standard components

15   were binding, and thus X Corp. bore the risk of loss for non-standard components pursuant to Section

16   4.4 of the MPA.

17          20.        In particular, during November and December of 2021, Inventec regularly checked in

18   with X to ensure that the parties were aligned on the 2022 forecast quantity. As early as November 8,

19   2021, Inventec sent a detailed email to X regarding purchasing raw materials to fulfill X’s request for

20   521 non-standard racks. In this same email, Inventec asked X to confirm if Inventec’s understanding

21   was correct and emphasized to X that Inventec needed to prepare raw materials for the non-standard

22   racks ahead of time given the supply chain constraints. On or around November 13, 2021, an X

23   employee, Marianne Gatmaitan, confirmed that Inventec should prepare the raw materials for X’s 521

24   non-standard racks demand. Thus, X Corp. understood that by approving the purchase of the needed

25   components, X Corp. was assuming liability for these components in the event that the components

26   were not used in the manufacture of the products forecasted by X Corp.

27

28

 1          21.     From December 2020 through early 2022, Inventec and X Corp. had a successful

 2   business relationship, with Inventec receiving and fulfilling multiple purchase orders from X Corp.

 3   for non-standard racks, based on X Corp.’s anticipated order forecast.

 4          22.     On or about April 19, 2022, X Corp. instructed Inventec to issue orders for switches to

 5   cover X Corp.’s forecast for 2022 through January 2023.

 6          23.     On or about April 20, 2022, X Corp. indicated a revised forecast for the 2022 year

 7   through January 2023 (“the 2023 Forecast”) of 505 non-standard server racks. In accordance with

 8   industry standard practices, as well as the course of dealing between the parties and the MPA, Inventec

 9   took steps to procure the components necessary to manufacture the non-standard server racks.

10          24.     On or about April 27, 2022, X Corp. confirmed that Inventec had placed purchase

11   orders for the switches.

12          25.     On or about June 15, 2022, X Corp. lowered its forecast for non-standard server racks

13   for the 2023 Forecast to 442, notwithstanding that Inventec had already moved forward with procuring

14   components necessary to manufacture and build the 505 server racks X Corp. previously projected.

15          26.     On or about July 26, 2022, X Corp. once again lowered the 2023 Forecast for non-

16   standard server racks to 215 racks. In particular, X Corp. indicated that it would require zero racks in

17   November 2022, and decreased the forecast for August, September, and October 2022 dramatically—

18   from 146 racks to 84 racks.

19          27.     On or around August 16, 2022, X Corp. and Inventec had a meeting to discuss the

20   excess inventory that X Corp. previously required Inventec to secure.

21          28.     On or around August 17, 2022, Inventec again raised the issue of the forecast decrease

22   for the non-standard server racks with X Corp.

23          29.     From August 2022 through October 2022, the parties discussed the forecast decrease

24   which resulted in Inventec having excess inventory. On or about October 4, 2022, X Corp. proposed,

25   and ultimately agreed, that it would purchase 168 non-standard server racks from Inventec, with

26   delivery no later than December 2022. Recognizing its liability for the non-standard components, X

27   Corp. made that proposal to “resolve[]…without any further obligation or liability to X Corp. ” claims

28   related to the “2022 forecasts.” X also requested that the purchase order for the 168 non-standard

      COMPLAINT                                         5
                                                                                                     110114977

 1   racks be executed within approximately the next 30 days, following the internal standard process for

 2   review and approvals. Inventec replied stating that they understood X’s required management

 3   approval as part of X’s internal process and asked X Corp.’s representative, Christopher Kan, to assist

 4   with facilitating the purchase order approval so Inventec could have it within two weeks, given that

 5   Inventec’s shipment and production had been suspended for several months. Mr. Kan responded

 6   asking Inventec to send quotes for the remaining 135 non-standard racks—which Inventec provided

 7   X Corp. with— and said that he would start working on the purchase order approval process. Mr. Kan

 8   also confirmed that he would be sending an agreement that formally documented the parties’ terms

 9   and conditions as discussed.

10          30.     The parties’ agreement was memorialized in an agreement (the “Rack Forecast

11   Agreement”) on or about October 18, 2022, when Mr. Kan confirmed that X Corp.’s chief executive

12   officer approved of the Rack Forecast Agreement orally and in writing. Pursuant to the Rack Forecast

13   Agreement, X Corp. was to issue one or more purchase orders to confirm delivery of the168 units. A

14   true and correct copy of the Rack Forecast Agreement is attached hereto as Exhibit C. A true and

15   correct copy of the email from Mr. Kan accepting the Rack Forecast Agreement on behalf of X. Corp.

16   is attached hereto as Exhibit B.

17          31.     Consistent with this Rack Forecast Agreement, Inventec shipped to X Corp. thirty-three

18   (33) of the agreed upon 168 racks pursuant to Purchase Order Nos. 10138087, 10140379, and

19   10140380. X Corp. took delivery and paid for them in accordance with the terms of the Rack Forecast

20   Agreement.

21          32.     On information and belief, on or about October 27, 2022, Elon Musk (“Mr. Musk”)

22   completed his acquisition of X Corp., at which time he became its chief executive officer (“CEO”).

23          33.     On information and belief, X Corp. did not formally execute the Rack Forecast

24   Agreement after giving affirmative assent to its terms because the intended signatory to the Rack

25   Forecast Agreement was unexpectedly terminated at Mr. Musk’s direction during the turmoil that

26   occurred at X Corp. following Mr. Musk’s purchase of X Corp.

27          34.     On information and belief, Mr. Musk intentionally created a chaotic environment at X

28   Corp. following his acquisition (including by terminating key personnel who were involved in

      COMPLAINT                                        6
                                                                                                    110114977
               Case 3:26-cv-05145      Document 1       Filed 05/29/26     Page 7 of 16




 1   commercial transactions with suppliers and vendors) in an attempt to refuse to honor X Corp.’s

 2   contractual obligations with certain of X Corp.’s vendors, including Inventec, among others.

 3            35.   On information and belief, X Corp., at Mr. Musk’s direction, attempted to renegotiate

 4   prices and contractual terms with certain of its vendors and suppliers, refusing to pay what it owed

 5   without good cause to do so.

 6            36.   Indeed, around the same time Mr. Musk was acquiring X Corp., Inventec was notified

 7   that the Rack Forecast Agreement was cancelled. When Inventec brought this up with Mr. Kan, he

 8   responded stating that “[t]he agreement was withdrawn and needed further review. My apologies.”

 9   Inventec replied asking for the status of the Rack Forecast Agreement and accompanying purchase

10   order because Inventec wanted to provide X Corp. with the requested non-standard racks as soon as

11   possible. On October 28, 2022, Mr. Kan responded that X Corp.’s “CFO was let go yesterday. He

12   was a key person in our agreement and PO process. I am waiting on further instructions from our

13   management team.” A true and correct copy of Mr. Kan’s October 28, 2022 correspondence is

14   attached hereto as Exhibit D.

15            37.   Despite its agreement to do so, X Corp. failed and/or refused to issue any purchase

16   orders for the other 135 of the 168 racks agreed to in the Rack Forecast Agreement (the “Agreed Upon

17   Racks”) in order to consume excess non-standard components. Inventec sent X Corp. an invoice for

18   the Agreed Upon Racks, confirming that X Corp. owes Inventec $31,735,789 for the Agreed Upon

19   Racks. Yet, X Corp. attempted to cancel its agreed-to obligation to purchase the Agreed Upon Racks.

20            38.   That is, X Corp. required Inventec to build non-standard racks with specific switches

21   for its benefit, a product which X Corp. was fully aware required a significant amount of lead time to

22   procure. X Corp. then failed to provide appropriate notice or good cause for significantly decreasing

23   the quantity of non-standard product it required, thereby damaging Inventec by requiring it to go out-

24   of-pocket by millions of dollars to build those non-standard racks for X Corp.

25            39.   X Corp. refused and continues to refuse to pay for the non-standard Agreed Upon

26   Racks.

27            40.   Additionally, in or about January 2023, Inventec sent X Corp. an invoice (“Invoice No.

28   U320001889”) in the amount of $1,729,954 for the switches (“Switches”) X Corp. had specifically

      COMPLAINT                                        7
                                                                                                    110114977
             Case 3:26-cv-05145         Document 1      Filed 05/29/26      Page 8 of 16




 1   instructed Inventec to purchase because of the approximate 1-year lead time associated with procuring

 2   those components. Inventec acquired the Switches in reliance upon X Corp.’s instructions.

 3          41.     X Corp. refused and continues not to pay for the Switches.

 4          42.     Inventec made multiple demands on X Corp. for payment on the combined balance of

 5   $33,465,743 due to Inventec for the Switches and Agreed Upon Racks.

 6          43.     X Corp. refused to pay the combined balance of $33,465,743 due to Inventec for the

 7   Switches and Agreed Upon Racks.

 8          44.     In addition to its attempts to resolve the issue of its excess non-standard components

 9   with X Corp., Inventec immediately attempted to mitigate its damages through various means,

10   including but not limited to cancelling approximately $12,086,527.00 worth of non-standard

11   components that had not yet been delivered to Inventec, attempting to sell the delivered but unused

12   components to other third parties, attempting to use the unused components in manufacturing products

13   for other Inventec customers, and attempting to repurpose the unused components for Inventec’s use

14   to absorb the relevant costs itself. Inventec has been able to recoup approximately $4.9 million by re-

15   selling and/or repurposing the unused components that were intended to be used in products for X

16   Corp. However, due to the nature of the components, Inventec has been and continues to be limited

17   in its ability to resell or reuse a substantial amount of components—which hold a significant total

18   value—despite Inventec’s best efforts. Accordingly, Inventec continues to be damaged in the amount

19   of at least $30 million for excess non-standard components that it procured for X Corp. but was unable

20   to dispose of through mitigation efforts after X Corp. breached its contractual obligations.

21          45.     Inventec has incurred and continues to incur significant storage and handling expenses

22   for the remaining unused components.

23          46.     Because it was left with no other options, Inventec files this action to recover from X

24   Corp. what X Corp. owes Inventec for the unused non-standard components.

25                                                 COUNT I

26                 (Breach of Contract Against X Corp. – Master Purchase Agreement)

27          47.     Inventec incorporates by reference and realleges paragraphs 1-46 above of this

28   Complaint as if fully set forth herein.

 1          48.      As stated above, X Corp. and Inventec entered into the Master Purchase Agreement,

 2   which is a valid and binding agreement.

 3          49.      Inventec has fully performed all its obligations under the Master Purchase Agreement.

 4          50.      X Corp. failed to properly compensate Inventec for the price of the excess non-standard

 5   components purchased by Inventec at the direction of X Corp. for the manufacture of non-standard

 6   products for X Corp., breaching Section 4.4 of the MPA as understood by the Parties, as evidenced by

11                13.3.      Termination for Convenience. Twitter may immediately terminate

                  to terminate.
